lignes.texte: The Dark Web is supposed to be a lawless frontier. An invisible space
the authorities can’t touch you. The truth is infinitely worse.
The state built it, they own the map, and they’re just waiting for you to cross the border.
For years, the world's most dangerous criminals thought they were untouchable,
trading billions in stolen data and crypto. But they weren’t hiding. They were walking
blindly into a trap. 10.
Dark websites such as Besa Mafia, Camorra Hitman, often advertising themselves as the
#1 Hitman Marketplace. They’ve even been called an “Etsy for hitmen.”
They can look surprisingly legitimate, offering services like the traditional bullet to the head.
But for the right amount of cash, a customer can order a bespoke package -- a variety of torture
that precedes a variety of kinds of murder. The Times newspaper in the UK reported that
just one of these websites had taken in over half a million dollars. Every cent
came from customers who had collectively paid for the assassinations of 175 people.
The people are genuine. The targets were real.
The hitman service wasn’t… well not always. It’s thought most of these sites no longer
function and everyone knows the vast majority are scams.
But people are still ordering murders on the Dark Web.
In 2025, Dutch journalists obtained hacked data from a Dark Web hitman site and discovered at
least 7 concrete orders to murder people in the Netherlands. Four customers had already paid up.
The intended victims weren't part of organized crime. One was a nurse. One was a teacher and
another a civil servant. The price paid for their death was between $1,200 and $11,700.
One of the customers wrote, “I want you to burn him alive,”.
Another client told the assassin he didn’t care if someone else got hurt in the crossfire:
“All I want is for him to die; I don’t care what happens to the mother.”
But here’s the thing. The police couldn’t be sure if all
these websites were fake. When a man named Imran M. ordered his ex-girlfriend nurse be killed,
even offering with a $500 bonus if they could do it at the weekend , the woman and her
family were forced into hiding for 6 months. You might have been told these sites are all
phony and police don’t fear anyone will actually die, but it’s always not the case. The contract
killing marketplace is alive and well and as a Dutch investigator told the press,
they take “these matters very seriously.” And it’s a problem that seems to be everywhere.
9. If you think the authorities
are only hunting hitmen overseas, think again. Dark Web assassins are being hired in the U.S., by
Americans who forget they have digital footprints. 38 year old Kristy Lynn Felkins sent Besa Mafia 12
bitcoins. If she’d waited and sold today, those coins would be worth over $929,000.
But instead of waiting to become a millionaire, she gave her coins to a fake hitman to have her
husband killed. She was willing to pay a $4,000 bonus if the assassin did it immediately.
Make it look like a mugging, she wrote, and told them not to worry about harming
her ex’s new lover. Money wasn’t an issue. Once he was dead, she’d come
into a very handsome life insurance policy. Felkins was using a hidden service on the
Tor network where the data is anonymized and users are supposed to be anonymous. But that
doesn’t matter if the website is breached and you’ve supplied the name and location
of your soon-to-be-assassinated husband. When a hacker calling himself “bRpsd”
hacked Besa Mafia and leaked the data of 250 user accounts, the FBI soon intervened. The agents read
almost 2,700 personal messages between admin and customers. Many were about the 38 hits that were
supposedly in process. There was even a “victims” folder with photographs of all the marks.
This time, the FBI knew that the website was a fake.
Some people believe the FBI itself creates these websites as honeypots
so they can prevent murders but so far that’s unconfirmed. Laws around entrapment
could make that difficult for them in court. But when hackers do the work for them: no problem.
Kristy Felkins got 5 years because ultimately, she believed the Dark Web would protect her identity.
As you’ll see throughout this video, that’s often not the case at all.
But first, let’s break the current trend of claiming that all Dark Web hitmen are
fake and tell you some stories about when they were 100% real.
8. That’s a lot of fake sites on
the Dark Web but the idea of using the internet to anonymously fund murder was originally very real.
It started with an American engineer and crypto-anarchist named Jim Bell. In the mid-1990s,
he wrote an essay titled Assassination Politics. He proposed anonymously crowdfunding the deaths
of government officials using encrypted digital cash, then in its infancy. No one would know who
had contributed the money or who had carried out the killing. According to Bell, the world would be
a better place without corrupt public officials. He wrote, “If only 0.1% of the population,
or one person in a thousand, was willing to pay $1 to see some government slimeball dead.”
He was serious. But it wasn’t until 2013,
when the Dark Web was in full flow, that someone calling themselves Kuwabatake
Sanjuro created the Assassination Market. Based on Bell’s idea, it included a system
where users predicted when someone would die. People contributed Bitcoin to a bounty on a
target and could secretly post the exact date that person would die. If
they were correct, they collected the bounty. There was, of course, one obvious way of making
sure your prediction came true… Kill the person yourself.
These weren’t imaginary targets, either. Bounties were reportedly placed on people including
Federal Reserve chairman Ben Bernanke, President Barack Obama and NSA director Keith Alexander.
Sanjuro was quite open about what he wanted to achieve, writing:
“I will be satisfied when all governments, all politicians, and all armies are destroyed.”
People made plenty of predictions but he gave up and took all the Bitcoin out once
it was worth well over a million dollars. This gave birth to the assassin-for-hire
phenomenon that together exposed that a lot of regular people were willing to pay
to have someone killed. But if you really wanted someone dead, you didn’t go to hitman websites.
You trawled Dark Web forums looking for wayward teens.
In 2018, two Russian men, aged 17 and 19, were arrested after assassinating
a top Russian investigator who was looking into a Dark Web drug trafficking operation.
The men had been hired after talking with a gang boss. They were paid in bitcoin and the victim,
Yevgeniya Shishkina, was gunned down on her doorstep outside her Moscow apartment.
One of the teens had posted his resume on a Dark Web site and that was how he ended up being
offered $15,000 in crypto for the hit. Both boys were not exactly skilled operators. One even had
to watch a YouTube video to see how to load the modified gun that he’d picked up at a dead-drop.
So, Dark Web hitmen are real… if you know where to look for them.
In 2021, 19-year-old Finn, Markus Aleksi Hytönen, didn’t post his resume to a Dark
Web forum but offered his services as a killer. He was contacted by 20-year-old Atu Viljami
Halonen who promised him the equivalent of about $11,000 to murder his father.
Hytönen went through with it. He stabbed and slashed the father
more than 40 times, all of which was watched by CCTV cameras. Police soon found out the 2
young men had met each other online and arranged the contract killing through the Tor network.
Both were eventually sentenced to life in prison: Hytönen for murder and Halonen for
soliciting it. According to Finnish broadcaster Yle, it was the first proven contract killing
in Finland to have been arranged online. So, Dark Web hitmen are not an urban legend.
And here’s something even more disturbing. In 2021, Italian police arrested a man who
had hired a Dark Web assassin to pour acid over his ex-girlfriend and leave her paralyzed. The
price? €10,000 in Bitcoin. Police intercepted the plot before she was harmed. Meanwhile,
Europol performed what it called an “urgent, complex crypto-analysis” that helped
identify who had bought the Bitcoin. They said that across Europe, organized
criminals have been turning to young, inexperienced men to carry out violence.
They warned in 2021 that the use of younger and inexperienced hitmen was becoming a serious issue.
Sometimes they’re recruited on the Dark Web. Sometimes through social media and encrypted
messaging apps, in what authorities have called violence-as-a-service.
Young people can be offered money -- sometimes tens of thousands -- to carry out shootings and
murders for criminals they’ve never even met. The 2 Russian killers and the teenagers in
Finland weren’t caught because someone had cracked Tor. They were caught because they were
amateurs who made ordinary forensic mistakes and failed to account for things like CCTV.
And there are plenty more kids just like them. As criminology professor David Wilson told
Harper’s in 2020, a surprising number of “economically desperate young men
are willing to take on these brutal jobs.” But compared to what you’re about to hear,
these teenage assassins are small-time players in the larger world of Dark Web crime.
7. In the 2010s,
Alexandre “Alex” Cazes, a 20-something-year-old Canadian, was living his “best life.”
He could be seen tearing around Thailand in a Lamborghini Aventador, sometimes at
terrifying speeds, while living with his Thai wife in a luxury home. He owned a Porsche,
properties in several countries, and millions of dollars in cryptocurrency.
By the age of 25, his own financial records put his net worth at $23 million.
Not bad for a college dropout. As a teenager growing up with his mother in
Trois-Rivières, Canada, Cazes had skipped a grade and was sometimes described as a “little genius.”
He studied computing at college but left to start his own IT business, EBX Technologies, building
websites, hosting servers and repairing computers. Then, at around 18 or 19, he moved to Thailand,
leaving what he called a “broken society” for something more traditional.
And it was from Thailand that the computer genius would build one of the biggest criminal
marketplaces on Earth: AlphaBay.
Launched in 2014 when Cazes was just 23, AlphaBay was essentially Amazon for the Dark Web.
Within 90 days, it reportedly had 14,000 users. By 2017, it had hundreds of thousands of users
and more than 250,000 listings for illegal drugs and toxic chemicals alone. You name it,
AlphaBay sold it. There were more than 100,000 listings for stolen identities, counterfeit goods,
hacking tools, fraudulent documents, firearms and many, many other illegal products.
An estimated $600,000 to $800,000 worth of transactions were taking place every single day.
AlphaBay had become even bigger than the Dark Web OG, Silk Road.
Cazes took commissions for the sales. That’s how he ended up driving a Lamborghini.
But while AlphaBay prided itself on security, its creator had made an
almost comically stupid mistake. The genius, it transpired,
was also a part-time idiot. When AlphaBay first started sending
welcome and password-reset emails, information hidden in the email headers exposed an address
belonging to its administrator: pimp_alex_91@hotmail.com
Not exactly the kind of anonymous email address you'd expect from the man operating
the world's nastiest marketplace. Investigators soon discovered that
Pimp_Alex_91 was associated with a Canadian computer programmer named Alexandre Cazes.
They then dug into the ancient internet and found posts Cazes had made on a
French-language computer forum back in 2008, when he was still a teenager. At the bottom
of one he'd helpfully left his real name: Alexandre Cazes: pimp_alex_91@hotmail.com
And the username he'd been posting under: Alpha02. Years later, the creator and administrator
of AlphaBay was using the name...you guessed it: Alpha02.
He had effectively left investigators a trail of breadcrumbs that led right to the
doorstep of his flash Bangkok home. Now they just needed to catch him…
preferably with his computer open. By 2017, investigators had secured
warrants and an international operation was underway. Canadian authorities were targeting
AlphaBay's infrastructure while Thai police, assisted by the FBI and DEA, prepared to arrest
Cazes at his Bangkok mansion. The cops were smart, though.
They didn’t just jump in. First, they created a service outage for AlphaBay
which meant Cazes had to access his computer and bring his empire back online. The alternatives
could have been him shutting everything down. On July 5th, Thai officers descended on his house.
Sure enough, his laptop was open and he hadn’t encrypted the information on it. He was actually
logged into AlphaBay as Admin. They caught him in the middle of trying to reboot the system and even
responding to messages from annoyed users. His empire had come crashing down.
Inside the computer, investigators found everything they needed. And if that wasn't enough,
Cazes had helpfully created what amounted to an inventory of his criminal fortune.
At the top it listed his total net worth, over £23 million. It also had his cryptocurrencies,
cash and more than $12.5 million worth of vehicles and real estate.
The police knew exactly what to seize. He was finished.
At 25 years old, the US now wanted him extradited on charges including racketeering,
narcotics distribution, identity theft, fraud and money laundering.
He never made it to the U.S. Just a week after his arrest,
Cazes was found dead in his jail cell. AlphaBay was dead.
Or so everyone thought... Because 4 years later, people began
receiving the message: AlphaBay is back in action! A mysterious figure calling himself DeSnake
was now the boss. He claimed he’d once been the original number-two
administrator and security specialist. Then the new DeSnake dropped a bombshell.
He was able to provide cryptographic evidence linking them to the old AlphaBay.
If it was an impostor, it was a convincing one. A smart one, too.
AlphaBay 2.0 incorporated new security mechanisms intended to allow the market
to survive even if its servers were seized. And so as not to pique the interest of police too much,
this version was almost ethical: no fentanyl, no porn, no COVID vaccines, no hitmen.
It seemed that even the Dark Web had standards. Or… DeSnake wasn’t who he said he was.
Maybe the new owner didn’t want to sell very dangerous items because…well…
DeSnake might be law enforcement. In February 2023, AlphaBay suddenly
went offline. DeSnake vanished and has never been heard from since.
Was he really the former AlphaBay administrator he claimed to be?
Or was he a law-enforcement honeypot catching criminals doing business on his marketplace?
Instead of spending years trying to identify criminals scattered across
the Dark Web, maybe the criminals came to them. It’s a theory, and as you’ll see now, there’s a
reason why many people believe it’s true. 6.
When the original AlphaBay went down in 2017 that left a lot of people
scrambling to get their fixes. But there was a solution.
Most sellers and buyers migrated to another Dark Web marketplace called Hansa.
But Hansa had one very serious flaw. The Dutch police had secretly taken
control of it. And they had studied the old administrators' communications
carefully enough to impersonate them perfectly. From being run by 2 old school cyber-criminals now
a group of hardworking officers were in charge. For customers, Hansa had never run so seamlessly.
One of the officers used work as an IT help-desk support. Now he’d taken over that part of Hansa he
very efficiently dealt with their complaints and resolved disputes between dealers and customers.
According to Gert Ras, head of the Dutch National High Tech Crime Unit:
“The quality really went up… Everyone was very satisfied with the level of service they got.”
For weeks, thousands of criminals fleeing their favorite marketplace were voluntarily
opening accounts on Hansa. After 27 days and approximately 27,000 transactions,
they shut it down… but for those 27 days, the investigators were having a blast.
Operation Bayonet, which encompassed all the operations we’ve talked about,
had given police the keys to the kingdom. They’d beaten the Dark Web at its own game.
So, was AlphaBay 2.0 police in disguise? We don’t know, but it was very possible.
Now let’s turn to one of the darkest aspects of this already dark corner of reality…
5. In January 2024,
hackers from the Rhysida ransomware group attacked Lurie Children’s Hospital in Chicago. Phone
numbers, email, electronic medical records and the patient portal went down. Doctors and staff were
forced back onto manual procedures. Appointments and surgeries were delayed or cancelled.
Why would anyone knowingly hurt children? Money.
Rhysida claimed to have stolen around 600 gigabytes of data and put it up for sale
on the Dark Web for 60 Bitcoin, worth about $3.4 million. The gang later claimed someone bought it,
although that was never independently confirmed. The breach affected a massive 792,000 people.
The stolen information potentially included names, addresses, dates of birth,
Social Security numbers, diagnoses, treatments, prescriptions and health insurance information.
In the hacking world, it was a goldmine. If someone steals your credit card details,
you call the bank. The card gets cancelled, you change your passwords
and another card arrives and life goes on. But you can’t change your date of birth.
You can’t easily change your Social Security number.
And you can’t change your medical history. Put all that information together and
criminals can use it for identity theft, fraudulent accounts, tax and insurance fraud,
or highly convincing phishing attacks. And, if the medical information is sensitive, blackmail.
This is fast-becoming a huge market on the Dark Web.
In 2024 alone, the US Department of Health and Human Services recorded 663 major healthcare
breaches affecting approximately 243 million individuals. Some people may have been counted
more than once, but the scale is still massive. A major study found that hacking
and IT incidents accounted for 91% of patient records exposed in healthcare breaches in 2024,
up from just 2% in 2010. It’s still happening.
In June 2026, hackers broke into Australian healthcare provider Partnered Health and stole
information from patients at 21 clinics. The data included all kinds of very private information.
One expert estimated that hackers could earn around $250 for every patient’s information.
Times that by many thousands or millions and someone can get very rich, very fast.
There’s also a huge legitimate data-broker industry collecting and selling information about
ordinary people. That information can be combined with data stolen in hacks allowing criminals to
build very detailed profiles of their victims. So while you might worry about someone stealing
your bank card, it’s your health data that they really want. You can pay $5 for credit card
information on the Dark Web and $250 to as much as $1,000 for health data. That’s 200 times more.
Once some of that information gets out, it stays out forever.
So let’s say you’re not a victim, but a customer. You think you’re safe in the digital shadows.
Well, you’re not. 4.
A very unpleasant fact of life is there are some extremely bad people on this planet we call home.
Around 1.2 million of them. That’s how many people were
members of a Dark Web pornography ring who used the website Welcome to Video. 4,000 of them were
paid members buying content. Spanning at least 38 countries, together they’d downloaded about
360,000 hours of video material. And it was some of the darkest,
most depraved material you can imagine. The customers thought they were getting
away with it. After all, they’d used a Dark Web website and paid for content with Bitcoin.
But even that cannot guarantee anonymity. Bitcoin's blockchain is a permanent public
ledger. It’s there for investigators to look at and advances in digital forensics are
improving all the time. Investigators use evolving deanonymization techniques in a process known as
identity resolution, aka, doxxing. That’s how Welcome to Video
customers were brought down. Police matched digital wallet
addresses to real-world identities and traced the website back to South Korea. They then arrested
a total of 337 people – most of them Koreans but also Americans, British, Germans, Spanish,
Saudi Arabian and dozens more nationalities. These people who’d mistakenly believed their
secret was safe with the Dark Web were not always obvious criminals. One of the arrested men was
Matthew Falder, a Cambridge-educated lecturer. Another was Gábor Kaleta, the Hungarian ambassador
to Peru. The haul of depraved Americans included Richard Gratkowski, a former Homeland Security
Investigations agent who it turned out had been investigated by his former place of work.
Deleting your account doesn't delete the blockchain. A transaction you
made years ago can become evidence when investigative technology catches up with you.
But let’s also remember that some people go to all the effort to hide themselves while making
very amateur mistakes. 3.
You might think these people doing bad things on the Dark Web are sophisticated.
After all, they’re already hiding themselves, but sometimes they make the most ridiculous mistakes.
The Welcome to Video investigation is proof. The case contains an almost unbelievable blunder made
by people who obviously didn’t understand how the Dark Web works. When the authorities were
investigating, they looked at the HTML source code of the supposedly hidden Tor website.
Tor uses what’s called onion routing – multiple layers of encryption that conceal your online
activity. Your data is wrapped in 3 layers and passed through 3 different servers. It’s like
giving a message to a friend who passes it to a stranger, who passes it to another stranger.
The first, called the entry node, knows who you are but not where you’re going. The middle node
passes the data along. The exit node knows where the data is going but not who originally sent it.
Each server only peels away its own layer of encryption, so no single server should know both
who you are and where you’re going. But in the Welcome to Video case,
the person running the site managed to undermine all that sophisticated
technology with an unbelievably amateur mistake. Hidden inside the website's source code was the
IP address of the actual server hosting some of its content. An investigator examining the site's
HTML noticed it. Police didn't need to crack Tor. The website itself had told them where to look.
Investigators traced the exposed IP address to a server in South Korea and that led them to
the front door of the site's administrator, Jong Woo Son. When police raided his home,
they reportedly found him sitting at his computer with the server running in his bedroom.
But here's where things get a little more complex. For this kind of system to work, you have to
trust that the different servers your data passes through aren't
secretly controlled by the same person. That sounds obvious, but it happened.
In 2021, a security researcher discovered that a mysterious entity known as KAX17 had
been operating hundreds of Tor relays since at least 2017. Nobody publicly knew who KAX17 was.
Nobody knew why he or she or they were doing it. At its peak, the group or person was reportedly
operating more than 900 Tor servers. That was about 14% of the network's guard capacity and
8% of its middle-relay capacity. They were essentially guarding the
front door and the hallways of the Dark Web. By controlling both ends of the chain, they
could instantly match traffic entering Tor with traffic exiting somewhere else. In the cyberworld
it’s known as traffic correlation. And it meant anonymity was dead.
It’s an incredible breakthrough if you’re an investigator. But for ordinary users who had
perfectly legal reasons to stay hidden - like journalists - KAX17 caused panic for people.
Tor's developers rushed to take down the suspicious relays, claiming there was no
evidence that any users were unmasked. So, no one got hurt… that we know of.
One theory is KAX17 was an intelligence agency. But if it really was harmless,
why did a phantom entity spend years - and a considerable amount of money - building it?
You don’t take over an anonymous global network just to do nothing.
There must have been a very good reason. We can’t talk about the Dark Web and leave
out drugs. 2.
Drugs are easily the biggest market on the Dark Web.
Nothing else comes close. In 2025, it’s believed $2.6 billion
worth was sold in the crypto-enabled illicit economy, a bumper year.
And there’s a reason for that. Research found that people buying
drugs through darknet markets reported less exposure to threats and violence compared to
people buying through traditional markets. Instead of meeting a dealer, you could now
access a marketplace through Tor and be presented with a menu of drugs and prices.
It was basically eBay for narcotics, complete with seller ratings and customer reviews.
And it became very popular. The 2019 Global Drug Survey found
that 28.6% of respondents had bought drugs from a Dark Web marketplace at some point in their lives.
It changed everything. Including the dealers.
Traditionally, selling drugs could require street cred, territory and the ability to
defend yourself. With the Dark Web, physical intimidation didn’t really matter. Anyone could
theoretically become a successful drug dealer without ever having to stand up for himself.
But more importantly, it introduced something unexpected to the illegal drug trade:
Customer satisfaction. Buyers could review dealers.
That created an incentive to sell what you actually advertised.
That doesn’t mean buying drugs on the Dark Web is anywhere near completely safe. Drugs can still
be contaminated or counterfeit, marketplaces can steal your money, police can be watching
and your package can be intercepted. Even so, this review system had for
the most part made a bad situation better. Studies have shown that Dark Web drugs can
sometimes be more reliable than street drugs and reliability can save lives.
But it’s not perfect. A study led by RMIT University
in Australia tested 103 illicit drugs bought through the Dark Web and found 35% weren’t
exactly what they were advertised as. Around 14% contained the advertised drug mixed with other
psychoactive or potentially harmful substances. 21% contained none of the advertised drugs at all.
Cocaine was particularly unreliable. Out of 19 samples, only 4 contained cocaine and nothing
else. 13 contained cocaine mixed with other substances and 2 contained no cocaine whatsoever.
On the other hand, every sample of heroin, MDMA and methamphetamine tested contained only what
the customer had been promised. Drugs sold as ketamine, 2C-B and alprazolam were among the most
likely to be something completely different. So, you think you’re guaranteed purity,
but that’s not always the case. Well, maybe not. A larger European
study tested 129 samples bought from Dark Web markets and found that 93% contained the
drug the customer thought they had purchased. And the coke was way stronger on the Dark Web,
averaging around 70% purity, compared to 38% for cocaine
seized on the streets in the UK at the time. Of course, stronger drugs create dangers of
their own. But knowing what substance you’ve actually bought and exactly how strong it is
removes at least one of the uncertainties of buying illegal drugs. Many deaths happen
because users don’t know what they’re getting. Dark Web markets even developed their own form
of harm reduction. Vendors and customers discussed purity, adulterants and safer use,
while bad products could receive bad reviews. But there is a darker side to making drugs
so easy to purchase. You could buy fentanyl.
You could even buy the vastly more potent carfentanil. Researchers have
identified dozens of vendors advertising carfentanil across Dark Web marketplaces.
At a time when people in Canada were dying from the drug,
one Dark Web customer left a 5-star review: “Took forever to find a new carfent supplier.
Finally found a good vendor!! Great!!!” Even so, if this person was going to
buy the drug anyway, maybe Amazon-style drug acquisition was safer than buying on the street.
Ok, so you might have heard your cryptocurrency is safe.
It’s not. 1.
In 2022, the Justice Department announced that it had seized more than 94,000 Bitcoin,
then worth about $3.6 billion. It was the largest financial seizure in its history.
The story goes back to 2016, when someone stole almost 120,000 Bitcoin
from the cryptocurrency exchange Bitfinex. At the time, the haul was worth about
$70 million but by 2022 that changed considerably. And the thief turned out to be quite a character.
His name was Ilya Lichtenstein. He worked alongside his wife, Heather “Razzlekhan” Morgan,
a woman who made quite possibly the worst rap music in existence. Morgan
would later admit helping launder the stolen money, but it was Lichtenstein
who had actually carried out the hack. So how did he steal that much Bitcoin?
Bitfinex thought it had built something like a vault requiring more than one key to open.
One layer of security was provided by an outside company called BitGo.
But Lichtenstein hacked deep enough into Bitfinex’s systems to fraudulently
authorize more than 2,000 withdrawals. In the process, thousands of Bitcoin were transferred
into a wallet under his control. Stealing it was one thing. Turning
billions of dollars of stolen Bitcoin into money you could actually spend without
getting caught was something else entirely. This is where the Dark Web enters the story.
Lichtenstein started feeding some of the stolen Bitcoin through AlphaBay. The idea was simple:
put dirty Bitcoin into a huge anonymous Dark Web marketplace,
move it around and withdraw Bitcoin elsewhere. It made the blockchain trail much harder to follow.
It might have worked well. Except, as you know,
the US government seized AlphaBay because the owner made those amateur mistakes.
So, instead of destroying the trail of the missing Bitcoin,
AlphaBay helped investigators reconstruct it. The Dark Web technology Lichtenstein had trusted
to help hide his billions had been made – and is still being funded – by the US government.
Onion routing was developed by researchers at the US Naval Research Laboratory to create
anonymous internet communications. Tor later became an independent nonprofit,
and inevitably drug dealers, hackers and stolen-data sellers jumped on the anonymity
bandwagon. But even with all the reported mayhem of the Dark Web, the US carried on funding Tor.
It still does. In 2023–24,
the Tor Project received around $2.56 million from US government sources, about 35% of its revenue.
So Lichtenstein had effectively used US-funded anonymity technology to help launder his potential
billions. And in part, cocaine aficionados demanding greater purity can also thank the
US government. But so can dissidents, journalists and even intelligence officers who have very good
reasons for wanting to remain anonymous. That’s the paradox.
One part of the US government spends billions trying to find criminals hiding on the Dark
Web. Meanwhile another spends millions supporting technology designed to make people harder to find.
Even if governments wanted to close down the Dark Web completely, that would be next
to impossible. Tor isn't a single website or company with a server someone can just unplug.
Shut down one marketplace and another appears. Take down one scammer and others take his place.
You can’t stop them. The Tor Project develops the software, but the network is decentralized,
with thousands of servers running independently all over the world.
And because the software is open-source, even if the Tor Project disappeared tomorrow, someone else
could pick up the code and keep it alive. In 2024, an estimated $1.7 billion in
cryptocurrency-enabled drug transactions went through the Dark Web. An increase
of 20% from the year before. No one knows how much stolen
information exists there because no one can take an inventory of it. But researchers have found 15
billion stolen usernames and passwords circulating through criminal markets,
about two for every human being on Earth. In 2025 alone, credentials from more than a
million accounts at the world's 100 largest banks were found being shared on Dark Web resources.
The Dark Web itself might be small compared with the regular internet but the amount of
stolen information circulating through it is anything but. So there’s a good chance that
information belonging to many of us has, at some point, ended up in a criminal database.
